en: The *Buddhabhāṣita-saṃgharakṣitotpattikathā-sūtra*, translated by an unknown person, now appended to the catalogue of the Eastern Jin dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, there was a dragon king of the great ocean who, having first conceived faith, transformed himself into human form and came to the grove to seek ordination in reliance upon the bhikṣus.
At that time, the bhikṣus did not know he was a nāga, so they immediately ordained him as a monk.
There was a young bhikṣu who lived in the same room; after one night had passed, at dawn, he assumed his dignified demeanor and went into the city to beg for alms.
At that time, due to the karmic fruit of his merit, the bhikṣu Nāga was the first to receive alms;
or else, having gone to his own palace, he would return early after eating.
It is the dharma of a bhikṣu to enter his cell after the meal and sit in meditation with a concentrated mind.
At that time, the bhikṣu Nāga had forgotten to close the door; moreover, nāgas by nature sleep much, and the weather was hot. There are five conditions under which a nāga cannot conceal its form:
first, at the time of birth;
second, at the time of death; [and so forth].
Third, at the time of sexual desire;
fourth, at the time of anger;
fifth, at the time of sleep—these are the five occasions. On these occasions, the bhikṣu Dragon was unable to conceal his body; he then fell asleep, his body filling the entire room.
A fellow monk entered the room later and saw only the dragon’s body filling the entire space; he was struck with great terror and fled in haste, crying out to the other monks:
"Venerable Elders! Venerable Elders!"
"There is a nāga king here!
There is a nāga king here!
Hearing this loud voice, the nāga immediately awoke and resumed his state as a bhikṣu, sitting cross-legged in meditation.
Because the sound was so loud that the great assembly gathered together and asked the young bhikṣu,
"For what reason are you raising your voice? The bhikṣu replied:
"There is a dragon in the room.

At that time, the great assembly immediately gathered together; they entered the room to search for the dragon but did not find it. Seeing instead the bhikṣu sitting cross-legged in meditation, they were greatly astonished and did not know why this was so.
He immediately went to question the Buddha, recounting the aforementioned events in detail and requesting a resolution for his doubts.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"This was not a human being!"
"This is indeed the Dragon King; you may go and summon him.
Having received these instructions, the bhikṣu summoned that Dragon King.
Thereupon, the bhikṣu-dragon went to where the Buddha was, prostrated himself with his head at the Buddha's feet, and withdrew to sit to one side.
The Buddha preached the Dharma for him, instructing, exhorting, benefiting, and gladdening him; the Buddha then remained silent.
At that time, the Dragon King reflected within his own mind and was filled with joy.
The Buddha consoled him, saying,
"You may return to your palace. Having heard this,
the Dragon King wept with sorrowful tears, prostrated at the Buddha's feet, circumambulated the Buddha three times, and then departed.
On the way, he reflected to himself:
"Although I have not yet been able to leave the household life, I shall act as a great donor within the Buddha-dharma, constructing monastic dwellings and providing the four requisites of support."

Having formed this thought, he immediately manifested at a desolate road a monastic dwelling, with flowing springs, ponds, marshes, and pleasure groves for strolling—extremely magnificent and tranquil, free from the clamor of crowds, where one could roam day and night, and moreover, devoid of insects, ants, mosquitoes, or gadflies.
Neither cold nor hot, it was temperate and comfortable, free from all afflictions and ailments.
He invited the assembly of monks, providing them with all necessary requisites—robes, food and drink, bedding, and medicinal decoctions—all of which were fully supplied.
The bhikṣus who upheld the Vinaya repeatedly rebuked him.
At that time, the dragon bhikṣu did not understand the sūtras or the precepts; he was constantly troubled by this and thought to himself:
"I now provide offerings and have prepared all necessary things, yet these bhikṣus still rebuke me."

He then caused the manifested temple to vanish and went to another empty place where he again manifested a temple; its palaces, groves, and springs were no different from the former one, and he again invited the assembly of monks to provide them with the four types of offerings.
Then the assembly of monks said to the bhikṣu Nāga:
"The inventory of the monastic storehouse contains a great many items; according to the rule for the temple master, you should calculate these items and present the count to the assembly."
The dragon then replied:
"Originally this was not the property of the Saṃgha; now you demand a written record, claiming that because it was made for [the Saṃgha], it is entirely my own possession.
Currently, it is difficult to provide for the bhikṣus."
"If it be so, you may endure this for a short while.
In the middle of the night, he extinguished the lamps in the monastery and returned to the palace.
At that time, there were five hundred merchants in the kingdom of Śrāvastī who had made a collective vow, intending to enter the great ocean.

The merchants deliberated together and sought out a Dharma Master to accompany them into the great ocean, so that they might inquire about the Dharma from time to time; by means of the benefits derived from hearing the Dharma, they could ensure a safe journey there and back.
Among the assembly of merchants, there was an elder who addressed the merchants:
"I have a teacher of mine named Saṃgharakṣita; you should invite him to be your teacher. He possesses eloquence and great wisdom, and is most capable of preaching the Dharma."
Then the merchants followed one another to go and invite him; having arrived at Saṃgharakṣita’s dwelling, they prostrated themselves with their heads at his feet and said to him:
“We wish to enter the great ocean. We now request the Venerable One to serve as our Dharma-preacher; by hearing the Dharma, we shall be able to return safely.”
Saṃgharakṣita replied, "You should inform the Upādhyāya; if the Upādhyāya permits it, I shall accept your invitation.
Then the bhikṣu Saṃgharakṣita led the merchants to where Śāriputra was, prostrated himself with his head at the elder's feet, and paid homage.
Then the merchants said to Śāriputra, “We, all of us, wish to enter the great ocean;
we now request Saṃgharakṣita to serve as our Dharma-preacher. We only pray that the Venerable One will grant us his permission.”
Śāriputra said, "We should go together to question the Buddha.

Then Śāriputra and the bhikṣu Saṃgharakṣita, leading the merchants, went to where the Buddha was, prostrated themselves with their heads at his feet, knelt for a long time with palms joined, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

We, all these people, wish to enter the great ocean; we request that the Venerable Saṃgharakṣita act as our Dharma-preacher so that we may inquire about the Dharma from time to time. By virtue of hearing the power of the Dharma, we shall be able to return safely.”
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing that the bhikṣu Saṃgharakṣita was destined to extensively deliver sentient beings, immediately granted his permission.
Then the merchants leaped for joy and, together with the Dharma Master Saṃgharakṣita, entered the great ocean; before they had reached the place of treasures, the Dragon King seized them.
At that time, the merchants were struck with great terror; kneeling on their right knees with palms joined, they looked up and asked:
"Which deity is this that has seized our ship and brought it to a halt?"
"If you wish to obtain [what you seek], you should manifest your physical form.
At that moment, the dragon king suddenly revealed his body.
Then, the merchants immediately asked:
"What do you seek? The Dragon King replied,
"Give this Bhikṣu Saṃgharakṣita to me."
The merchant replied, “This Bhikṣu Saṃgharakṣita requested it from the World-Honored Buddha and from Śāriputra; how could we give it to him?”
The Dragon King replied,
"If you do not give it to me, I shall submerge and kill you all.
At that moment, the merchants were struck with great terror and immediately reflected upon a verse they had previously heard from the Buddha:
"To protect a single family, one would rather abandon a single person;
to protect a single village, one would rather abandon a single family;
to protect a single kingdom, one would rather abandon a single village."
"To protect our lives, we would rather give up our kingdom and wealth.
Then the merchants, after much deliberation, surrendered the bhikṣu Saṃgharakṣita to the dragon king.
The Dragon King was filled with joy and led him into his palace.
At that time, the Dragon King took four dragons—endowed with intelligence and wisdom—as Saṃgharakṣita’s disciples.
The Dragon King addressed him, saying:
"Venerable One! Please instruct these four dragons; each has a portion of the Āgamas."
The first dragon was taught the Ekottarika Āgama;
the second dragon was taught the Madhyama Āgama;
the third dragon was taught the Saṃyukta Āgama.
"The fourth dragon teaches the *Dīrgha Āgama*.
Saṃgharakṣita replied, "Very well; I shall study it."
The bhikṣu Saṃgharakṣita then instructed them.
The first nāga listened in silence;
the second nāga, with eyes closed, recited it orally.
The third dragon looked back to listen and receive;
the fourth dragon stayed at a distance to listen and receive.
These four dragon sons were clever and wise; within six months, they recited the four Āgamas, taking them all into their hearts without leaving out a single detail.
Then the Great Dragon King went to where Saṃgharakṣita was, prostrated himself, and inquired after his well-being, asking:
"Are you not distressed? Saṃgharakṣita replied:
"I am deeply distressed.
The Dragon King asked,
"For what reason are you distressed?"
Saṃgharakṣita replied:
"One who upholds the Dharma must necessarily observe the rules of discipline.
These nāgas, being in the realm of animals, lack a disciplined mind; they do not know the Buddha-dharma, nor do they practice its reception, retention, recitation, or study."
The Dragon King said:
"Venerable Sir,
you should not reproach the dragons."
Why is this? It is for the sake of protecting the life of the teacher.
A dragon possesses four poisons; therefore, one must not receive, uphold, read, or recite [the teachings] according to the Dharma [in their presence].
Why did he accept in silence?
Because the sound would have been poisonous and thus not in accordance with the Dharma;
had he made a sound, it would surely have endangered the Master’s life. For this reason, he accepted in silence.
As for the recipient who closes his eyes, because he perceives the poison of [the teacher's] views, he cannot practice according to the Dharma;
if he were to see the teacher, he would surely harm the teacher’s life; therefore, he closes his eyes.
Regarding the recipient who looks back: because of the poison of their breath, they cannot receive [the gift] according to the Dharma;
if they were to breathe upon the teacher, it would surely endanger his life—therefore, they look back.
Regarding the recipient who stays at a distance: because of the poison of physical contact, they cannot receive [the gift] according to the Dharma.
"If I were to touch the master with my body, I would surely take his life; therefore, I remain at a distance.
At that time, the merchants who had been gathering treasures returned and arrived at the place where they had lost their master.
At that time, the merchants said to one another:

"We originally lost our leader here; now, if we return to the presence of the Buddha, the World-Honored One, and the venerable elders such as Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana ask us about the Dharma Master Saṃgharakṣita, how shall we answer?"
At that time, the Dragon King, knowing that the merchants were returning, immediately entrusted Saṃgharakṣita back to them and said to the merchants,
"This is your teacher, the bhikṣu Saṃgharakṣita."
At that time, the merchants leaped for joy and emerged in safety.
Then, Saṃgharakṣita asked the merchants,
"Of the two routes, by water and by land, which way shall we go?"
The merchants replied, "The water route is extremely long;
it takes six months to traverse, and our provisions will be exhausted before we can reach our destination.
They then deliberated together on what was appropriate and set out by the land route.
While staying overnight along the way, the bhikṣu Saṅgharakṣita said to the merchants:
"I shall stay apart from the group; you must set out at night and call out to me with loud voices."
The merchants respectfully agreed.
The bhikṣu Saṃgharakṣita then left the assembly to stay overnight; he sat in meditation during the first watch of the night and slept during the middle watch.
At that time, the merchants set out during the middle watch, calling out to one another for the teacher Saṃgharakṣita, yet as no one called him, they simply departed.

As the night was drawing to a close, a great wind and rain arose; the bhikṣu Saṃgharakṣita immediately awoke, cried out at the top of his voice, but there was no one who answered him. He thought to himself:
"This is a grave misfortune; my companions have abandoned me."
At that time, the bhikṣu Saṃgharakṣita lost his companions and went alone. Before he had traveled far along the road, he heard the sound of a *ghanṭā* (gong).
Following the sound toward the monastery, he encountered a man on the way and immediately asked him:
"For what reason is the *ghanṭā* being struck?"
The man replied, "I am entering the warm bathhouse to bathe.
Saṃgharakṣita thought to himself:
"I have come from afar and may avail myself of the bath with the Saṃgha.
He then entered the monastery and saw a group of people who appeared to be monks, all entering the heated bathhouse together.
He saw all the bathing implements, bathing robes, earthen jars, and basins, as well as the entire bathhouse, engulfed in flames.

At that time, the bhikṣu Saṃgharakṣita saw the other bhikṣus enter the heated chamber together; once inside, it was ablaze, their flesh and sinews completely consumed, leaving their bones like charred wicks.
Saṃgharakṣita was struck with fear and asked the bhikṣus,
"Who are you? The bhikṣus replied:
"The people of Jambudvīpa are by nature difficult to convince.
When you reach the Buddha's presence, you may then question the Buddha.
Thereupon, [the monk] became terrified and fled from the monastery.

Before he had traveled far, he encountered another monastery. This monastery was magnificent and exceptionally well-crafted; he again heard the sound of a *kiṃśuka* drum and saw a bhikṣu. He immediately asked him:
"For what cause and condition is the *kiṃśuka* drum being struck?"
The bhikṣu replied, “The community of monks is eating rice.
He then reflected to himself:
"I have come from afar and am now extremely hungry and exhausted; I also require food.

Having entered the monastic quarters, he saw that the monks were gathered together, and the eating vessels and bedding were all ablaze; the people and the dwellings were entirely consumed by fire, no different from before.
Saṃgharakṣita asked, "Who are you? The person replied:
"It is no different from before.
Saṃgharakṣita was struck with alarm and fled even more swiftly.
Before he had traveled far along the road, he encountered another monastery; its solemn appearance was again no different from the previous one.

Entering the monastic quarters once more, he again saw various bhikṣus sitting on fire-beds, scratching and beating one another until their flesh was gone and their ribs were exposed; their five viscera and marrow were like scorched wicks.
Saṃgharakṣita asked, "Who are you? The bhikṣu replied:
"The people of Jambudvīpa are by nature difficult to convince.
When you reach the Buddha’s presence, you may then question the Buddha.
Monksaṃgharakṣita was struck with alarm and fear, and he quickly departed.
Before they had traveled far, they encountered another monastery; entering it as before, they saw the various monks sitting together and eating.
The bhikṣus said, "You must leave now."

Saṃgharakṣita hesitated and had not yet gone out when he saw that the bowls of the bhikṣus contained nothing but human excrement, which was boiling and bubbling over as the bhikṣus were all devouring it.
Having eaten, fire burned his throat and five internal organs, turning them all into smoke and charcoal as they passed straight through him.
Seeing this, he was struck with terror and fled swiftly once more.
Before he had gone far, he saw another monastery; its solemn grandeur was no different from the one before.
He immediately entered the monastic quarters and saw various bhikṣus holding iron hammers in their hands, striking one another until they were crushed to dust.
Having seen this, he was struck with terror and proceeded further along his path.
Not long after he had departed, he saw another monastery; it was magnificent and no different from the previous one.
He immediately entered the monastic quarters and heard the sound of the *gandi* drum.
Saṅgharakṣita asked,
"For what reason are you striking the wooden gong? The bhikṣus replied:
"I wish to drink sweet syrup.
The bhikṣu Saṃgharakṣita then thought to himself:
"I am now parched with thirst; I must drink sweet syrup."
He immediately entered the midst of the assembly and saw various food vessels, beds, and bedding.
The bhikṣus were reviling one another, and their food vessels were filled to the brim with molten copper.

All the bhikṣus together partook of the food; having eaten, it ignited their throats and five internal organs, turning them all into glowing coals that passed straight through as they flowed downward.
Having seen this, they were struck with terror and proceeded on their way.
Not long after he had departed, he saw a vast expanse of flesh, its flames blazing fiercely; there were cries of wailing and agony, and the suffering was unbearable.
Having seen this, he was struck with terror and pressed onward on his path.
Before he had gone far, he again saw the great earth, no different from before.
Proceeding further still, he saw a large vat of flesh, all ablaze with fire; its burning heat and pain were unbearable, just as before.
Advancing further still, he again saw jars of flesh, all ablaze with fire, no different from before.
Advancing yet further, he saw a jar of flesh; its flames were fiercely burning, and the cries of suffering were heard as the agonizing pain was unbearable.
Advancing further still, he saw a jar of flesh, its flames blazing as intensely as before, no different from what he had seen previously.

Advancing yet further, he saw a great spring of hide; its flames were fiercely burning, and the boiling hides overflowed with such intensity that the sounds of suffering and agony were no different from those heard before. Having seen this, he was struck with terror.
Proceeding further on his way, before he had traveled far, he saw another great vat of flesh, its flames blazing fiercely; the suffering there was as described before.

Proceeding yet further, he saw a bhikṣu holding a sharp blade in his hand, cutting off his own nose. Once cut off, it grew back again; once grown, he cut it off again, beginning and ending this cycle over and over without rest.
Advancing further still, he saw a bhikṣu holding an adze in his hand, cutting out his own tongue, beginning again and again from where he had finished, no different than before.
Advancing further still, he saw a bhikṣu standing alone in water, chanting aloud by himself:
"Water, water," without ceasing.
Thus they suffered bitter agony.
Proceeding further still, he saw a bhikṣu within an iron thorn grove, standing upon iron thorns, wailing with cries of pain no different from those before.
Advancing further still, he saw a hall of flesh, its flames blazing fiercely; the cries of suffering were no different from those before.
Advancing yet further, he saw a stake of flesh shaped like an elephant tusk, its flames blazing fiercely, and the suffering therein was as it had been previously.
Advancing further still, he saw a camel whose body was scorched by fire; it wailed in agony, no different from what had been seen before.
Advancing yet further, he saw a horse whose body was scorched by fire; it cried out in pain, no different from what had been seen before.
Advancing further still, he saw a white elephant whose body was engulfed in blazing fire; its suffering was no different from before.
Advancing yet further, he saw a donkey whose body was consumed by fierce flames; its suffering was no different from before.
Advancing further still, he saw a ram with its body engulfed in fierce flames; its suffering was no different from before.
Advancing yet further, he saw a mound of flesh, intensely ablaze with great flames; its suffering was no different from before.
Advancing further still, he saw a mound of flesh, no different from before.
Advancing yet further, he saw a chamber of flesh where beings were being burned by fierce fires; their cries of agony and lamentation were likewise no different from those heard previously.
Advancing further still, he saw a forest of flesh, where beings wailed with cries of suffering no different from those before.
Advancing yet further, he saw a bed of flesh, its bodies scorched by flaming fires, likewise no different from what had come before.
Advancing further still, he saw a scale of flesh being stretched and contracted by fire; its suffering was no different from before.
Advancing further still, he saw a pair of flesh-tongs being stretched and contracted by fire; its suffering was no different from before.
Advancing further still, he saw a fleshly couch being scorched by fire and suffering, which was no different from what he had seen before.
Advancing yet further, he saw a fleshly wall being scorched by fire and trembling, its suffering no different from what he had seen before.
Advancing further still, he saw a rope of flesh being stretched and contracted by fire; his suffering was no different from before.
Advancing further still, he saw a latrine well in which excrement and urine were surging and boiling; his suffering was no different from before.
Proceeding further still, he saw a high seat upon which sat a bhikṣu, sitting upright with his mind concentrated; though a fierce fire was burning him, his cries of suffering were as before.
Proceeding further still, he again saw a high seat where suffering bhikṣus were likewise no different from those before.
Proceeding further still, he saw a flesh-drum being scorched by fire, its cries of agony likewise no different from those before.
Advancing further still, he saw a fleshly *hukhi-chi*—the local name for which is *kūṣmāṇḍa*—whose body was scorched by fierce fires, suffering as before.
Advancing yet further, he saw a fleshly *kūṣmāṇḍa*, suffering as before.
Advancing further still, he saw a great mountain of flesh, scorched by fierce fires, trembling and roaring; its suffering was no different from before.
Advancing yet further, he saw *sumanā* flower trees, burning with fire and undergoing suffering, which likewise was no different from before.
Advancing further still, they again see *sumanā* flower trees; when burned by fire, they emit sounds no different from those before.
Advancing yet further, they see flesh-flower trees; when burned by fire, the suffering produced is no different from that before.
Proceeding further still, he saw a tree bearing fruit of flesh; the sound of its burning and the suffering therein were no different from before.
Proceeding yet further, he saw another tree, where the fire burned and suffering was endured, likewise no different from what had come before.
Advancing further still, he saw a pillar of flesh being burned with fire and suffering pain no different from before.
Advancing yet further, he saw another pillar of flesh, which the hell-wardens were hacking with axes, suffering as they had before.
Advancing further still, he saw a pillar of flesh being burned by fire and suffering, which was no different from what he had seen before.
Advancing further still, he saw fourteen trees of flesh being burned by fire and suffering, which were likewise no different from what he had seen before.

Advancing further still, he saw two bhikṣus striking each other with clubs; their heads were split open and their brains shattered, from which pus and blood flowed out. Once exhausted, they would regenerate, beginning again after the end, their suffering never ceasing.

The bhikṣu Saṃgharakṣita advanced a short distance further and saw two śrāmaṇeras lying asleep, embracing one another, their bodies being consumed by fierce flames, suffering without respite. Having seen this,
the bhikṣu Saṃgharakṣita was struck with fear and asked the śrāmaṇeras,
"Who are you that undergo such suffering?"
The śrāmaṇera replied,
“The people of Jambudvīpa are by nature difficult to convince.
When you have reached the World-Honored One’s presence, you may ask the Buddha yourself.”
Having seen this, he was struck with fear.

Continuing further on his way, he saw from afar a grove of trees, lush and delightful; he proceeded toward it and entered the forest, where he saw five hundred sages dwelling and moving about within the woods.
When the seers saw the bhikṣu Saṃgharakṣita, they fled in all directions to avoid him, saying to one another,
"The disciples of Śākyamuni are defiling our grove.
The bhikṣu Saṃgharakṣita borrowed a tree from the seers to stay for one night, intending to depart early the next morning.
Among the assembly of rishis, the foremost elder, possessing great compassion, commanded the junior rishis:
"Lend a tree to this śramaṇa.
The bhikṣu Saṃgharakṣita immediately obtained a tree; beneath it, he spread out his sitting mat (niṣīdana) and sat down cross-legged.
During the first watch of the night, he subdued and extinguished the five hindrances;
during the middle watch, he slept and rested;
during the final watch, he sat upright and chanted aloud with a resonant voice.

At that time, when the various seers heard the sound of the chanting, they realized the emptiness of intrinsic nature and attained the fruit of non-returning (anāgāmiphala). Seeing the Dharma with joy, they went to where the śramaṇa was, prostrated themselves at his feet, and requested of the śramaṇa that they receive the three refuges. They then sought to leave the household life within the Buddha-Dharma.

At that time, the bhikṣu Saṃgharakṣita immediately ordained the rishi, causing him to leave the household life according to the Dharma. He instructed him in the practice of dhyāna, and before long he attained meditative concentration and realized the fruit of arhatship. Like sandalwood surrounded by sandalwood, the bhikṣu who had attained the Way became a noble and holy member of the assembly.

At that time, the bhikṣu Saṃgharakṣita, together with his disciples, went to the Jetavana Monastery in the kingdom of Śrāvastī. Upon arriving at the place where the Buddha was, he prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet and withdrew to sit to one side.
At that time, the World-Honored One comforted the bhikṣus:
"Did you not suffer fatigue on your journey?
Was it easy for you to obtain almsfood?"
At that time, the bhikṣu Saṃgharakṣita addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
We have not been greatly fatigued or distressed by our journey; alms were easily obtained and we did not experience weariness, so that we have now been able to see the World-Honored One."
At that time, the World-Honored One was preaching the essentials of the Dharma for the great assembly.
Then, the bhikṣu Saṃgharakṣita, before the World-Honored One and amidst the great assembly, cried out in a loud voice, recounting the causes and conditions of the hells he had previously witnessed:
"I pray only that the World-Honored One will explain to me the original causes and conditions."
The Buddha told Saṃgharakṣita:
"Those bhikṣus and the bathhouse you previously saw are not bhikṣus, nor are they a bathhouse; they are inhabitants of hell."

These sinful persons were, during the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, ordained bhikṣus who did not rely upon the Vinaya, but followed their own ignorant inclinations; they used the bathing implements and various utensils belonging to the Saṃgha according to their own whims, and when the bhikṣus who upheld the Vinaya constantly instructed them in the proper rules, they did not comply with those teachings.
"Since the parinirvāṇa of Kāśyapa Buddha, they have endured the sufferings of hell without ceasing even until now.
The Buddha told Saṃgharakṣita:
"That monastery you first saw was not a monastic temple, nor were those monks; they were inhabitants of hell."

During the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, this person was a renunciant who failed to cultivate the five virtues. Regarding the property of the Sangha from the four quarters, he did not strike the *gandi* bell before using it, but instead shared it with the assembly in silence. Due to these causes and conditions, he now undergoes the suffering of the flaming bed.
"Since the parinirvāṇa of Kāśyapa Buddha, they have undergone the sufferings of hell, which continue unabated until now.
As for the second temple you see, it is neither a monastery nor do those within it belong to the saṃgha; they are inhabitants of hell."

During the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, this person was an ordained monastic who lacked the five virtues; nevertheless, various donors constructed a monastery for him, providing the four requisites in abundance.
When the donor first established the monastery, he intended to provide for all beings by striking the *ghanṭā* (bell).
Yet these bhikṣus did not strike the *ghanṭā*, and they consumed the offerings in silence; consequently, when visiting bhikṣus arrived, they received no food or drink and departed with empty bowls.
For this reason, they suffer the agony of fiery beds, clawing and beating one another until their flesh and sinews are completely consumed and their bones resemble scorched wicks.
Since the parinirvāṇa of Kāśyapa Buddha, they have endured such suffering, which continues unabated to this day.
"That which you see as the third monastery is not a monastic establishment for the Sangha, nor are those there bhikṣus; they are inhabitants of hell.
During the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, these were renunciants who were indolent bhikṣus living together in great numbers. They said to one another:
'We should now jointly invite a bhikṣu who upholds the Vinaya so that we may perform the ritual services together in accordance with the Dharma.'"
He immediately searched for and found a bhikṣu of pure conduct with whom he lived, ate, and slept.
This bhikṣu of pure conduct, in turn, searched further for a fellow-practitioner bhikṣu.
At that time, as the practitioners of pure conduct increased more and more, they pursued [the others] and forced them out of the monastery.
Then, during the night, those who had broken the precepts set fire to the monastery and extinguished all the bhikṣus.
For this reason, they grasp iron hammers and strike one another down to mutual destruction.
Since the parinirvāṇa of Kāśyapa Buddha, they have endured great suffering and affliction, which continues unabated to this day.
"That which you see as the fourth temple is not a monastery for the Sangha, nor are those there bhikṣus; they are inhabitants of hell.

During the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, they were renunciants who resided permanently within a monastery. When various donors brought offerings of fat and meat, it was their duty to distribute them among those present."
At that time, a visiting monk arrived; because of his stingy mind, the resident monks waited for the guest to leave before they intended to divide the food.
Before they could even begin the division, worms emerged and the food became putrid and foul-smelling, so they discarded it outside.
For these reasons, they entered hell and eat excrement and filth as food.
Since the parinirvāṇa of Kāśyapa Buddha, they have suffered without ceasing.
"As for what you see as the fifth temple, it is not a monastery of the Saṃgha, nor are those there bhikṣus; they are inhabitants of hell."
During the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, this person was an ordained monk who, while at the meal, ate improperly and reviled others with harsh speech.

Due to these causes and conditions, he now undergoes the suffering of the iron bed; within all the food vessels, boiling fire flows everywhere, his flesh and sinews are completely consumed, and his bones are like charred wicks.
"From the time of the parinirvāṇa of Kāśyapa Buddha until the present, it has never ceased.
As for what you see as the sixth temple, it is not a monastery for the Saṃgha, nor are those there bhikṣus; they are inhabitants of hell."
During the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, this renunciant did not strike the *gaṇḍī* bell, but instead silently shared sweet gruel with the community of monks, fearing that other monks might arrive.
Due to these causes and conditions of stinginess, he fell into hell, where he must drink and swallow molten copper.
"Since the parinirvāṇa of Kāśyapa Buddha, they have suffered here without ceasing until now.
At that time, the Buddha again addressed the bhikṣu Saṃgharakṣita:
"That which you see as the first ground is not the great earth; it is a person in hell."
During the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, this person was a renunciant who planted crops for his own private use in the fields belonging to the Saṃgha without compensating the community for their value.
A bhikṣu who upheld the Vinaya reprimanded him in accordance with the precepts:
"Why do you now fail to compensate the Saṃgha for its value?"
At that time, relying on the power of the king, this man did not accept their instruction and replied to the bhikṣus:
"Am I your slave? If you have the strength, why do you not plant for yourselves?"
"By these causes and conditions, they undergo the sufferings of the great hells.
From the time of the parinirvāṇa of Kāśyapa Buddha until now, this has not ceased.
As for what you see as the second earth, it is not actually earth; it is rather the sinners themselves."
During the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, this layperson cultivated the field of the Sangha but did not pay the Sangha for its value.
Because of these causes and conditions, he fell into hell and became a great mound of flesh, undergoing various sufferings that continue unabated to this day.
"As for what you saw as the first jar of meat, it was not a jar of meat but rather a sinner.

During the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, he was the senior monk (upādhyāya) of this community of monks; yet he was unable to practice meditation or recite the scriptures, nor did he understand the Vinaya. He ate his fill and slept soundly, engaging only in useless discourse, and when fine delicacies were offered as alms, he consumed them before the others."
Because of these causes and conditions, they entered hell and became great flesh cauldrons, suffering from being scorched by fire, which continues unabated to this day.
"The second cauldron you see is not actually a cauldron; it is a person from hell."

During the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, this person was an ordained monk who lacked the five virtues. Although he served as the kitchen supervisor for the Sangha, he consumed the soft and delicious offerings for himself first, while distributing the coarse, gritty, and poor-quality food to the assembly of monks.
Because of these causes and conditions, they entered hell and became great cauldrons of flesh, suffering as they were scorched by fire, which continues unabated to this day.
"That which you saw as the third cauldron is not a cauldron; it is a person from hell."

During the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, this person was a monastic attendant (*śrāmaṇera*). When preparing food and drink, he would first taste and eat the finest and most delicious portions, or give them to his wife and children; as for the coarse, bitter, and inferior portions, he would take these and distribute them among the Sangha.
"By these causes and conditions, you have been born in hell as a great vessel of flesh, suffering from being burned by fire, which continues unabated until this day.
At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed the bhikṣu Saṃgharakṣita:
"That which you see as the first jar is not a jar; it is a person in hell."

During the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, this renunciant served as the kitchen supervisor for the Saṃgha; he would set aside food intended for the morning meal until the following day, and food intended for that following day until the third day.
"By these causes and conditions, they enter into hell and become great vessels of flesh, suffering as they are scorched by fire without ceasing even until now.
As for what you see as the second vessel, it is not a vessel; it is a person from hell."

During the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, there was a renunciant who resided permanently at a monastery. Various donors presented jars of ghee as an offering for the assembly of monks present, which was to be divided among everyone.
This person, when seeing visiting monks, would hide them away in the back; only after the visitors had departed would he then divide the food.
Because of these causes and conditions, he has entered hell and become a great vessel of flesh, suffering from being burned by fire without ceasing even until now.
"The person you see standing in the water is not a bhikṣu; he is a being from hell.

During the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, he was a renunciant who served as the water-distributor for the Saṃgha. Seeing the monks using water, he would give them only a small amount, yet when it came to those he favored, he would immediately provide them with enough water, while the remainder were not given anything at all."
Due to these causes and conditions, he entered hell and stands alone amidst the water, crying out "Water! Water! as he undergoes great suffering that continues without end to this day.
"That which you see as a large jar is not a jar; it is a person from hell.

During the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, this individual was a renunciant who served as the monastery steward. He would first eat for himself the fruits, vegetables, and fragrant delicacies that were most excellent, while giving the sour fruits and bitter vegetables to others according to his own whims. Because he acted with such inequality, [he has now been reborn here]."
Because of these causes and conditions, they have entered into hell and been made into great flesh jars, suffering from being burned by fire without ceasing even until now.
"The bhikṣu you saw whose nose was cut off with a blade was not a bhikṣu; he was a person from hell."
During the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, this person was an ordained monk who snot and spat upon the pure ground of the Buddha’s saṃgha.
Due to these causes and conditions, he entered hell, where his nose was sliced off with knives and he suffered being burned by fire, which continues unabated to this day.
"You see this bhikṣu holding an axe in his hand and cutting out his own tongue; he is not a bhikṣu, but a person from hell.

During the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, he was an ordained śrāmaṇera who, while serving the community of monks, was to distribute rock honey. He cut it into several pieces, and with a small amount of honey still clinging to the edge of the axe, the śrāmaṇera licked it off."
"By these causes and conditions, he has endured the suffering of having his tongue cut off, which continues unabated to this day.
At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed the bhikṣu Saṃgharakṣita:
"That which you see as a spring is not a water spring; it is a person from hell."

During the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, this person was an ordained śrāmaṇera who served honey for the Saṃgha; he first tasted and ate it himself, and later gave the remainder to the assembly of monks, so that it was diminished and not distributed to all.

Because of these causes and conditions, he entered hell and became a great pool of flesh, where he was scorched and boiled by fire, undergoing great suffering and distress that even now has not ceased.
“The bhikṣu you see standing upon the stake is not a bhikṣu; he is a person from hell.
During the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, he was an ordained renunciant who used harsh speech to revile and abuse other bhikṣus.”
"By these causes and conditions, they have entered the hells and stand upon iron spikes, suffering as they are scorched by fire without ceasing even until now.
What you see as a meat canopy is not a canopy; it is a person from the hells."

During the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, this person was a renunciant who resided permanently in a monastery. Lacking the five virtues, he served as the kitchen steward for the Saṃgha; he would eat the finest and most delicious food himself, or sometimes give it to laypeople to eat. With a mind full of partiality toward high and low, he distributed [the remaining food] to the members of the Saṃgha.
Because of these causes and conditions, they undergo the sufferings of hell, which continue without ceasing even until now.
"That which you see as a stake is not actually a stake; it is a person from hell."

During the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, this person was an ordained monk who resided permanently in a monastery; he drove various wooden stakes into the walls of the monastic compound for his own purposes, not for the sake of the Sangha, in order to hang his own robes and bowl.
"By these causes and conditions, they entered the hells and became large meat stakes, suffering from being burned by fire without ceasing even until now.
At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed Saṃgharakṣita:
"That which you saw as a camel is not actually a camel; it is a person from the hells."

During the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, this person was an ordained monk who served as the senior elder (sthavira) of a monastery; he regularly received his portion of food, sometimes receiving the portions intended for one or two people.
The bhikṣu who upholds the Vinaya instructed him according to the Dharma, saying:
"The practice of an elder should not be like this.
At that time, the old bhikṣu replied to the Vinaya-master:

"You know nothing; your voice is like that of a camel. Among this assembly, I am the senior elder (*sthavira*), and when I offer prayers, preach the Dharma, or occasionally perform hymns (*geya*), I deserve to receive my due for such labor. Why do you all constantly scold and reproach me?"

"Because of these causes and conditions, he entered hell and received the body of a camel; he suffers the agony of being burned by fire and crying out in distress, which has not ceased even until now.
'The horse you saw was not actually a horse; it was a person from hell.'"

During the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, he served as a monastery attendant (śrāmaṇera). He used the monastic offerings for his own excessive consumption, or gave them to his relatives, acquaintances, and laypeople.
The bhikṣus rebuked him, saying,
"You should not act in this way.
That man, with harsh words, reviled the bhikṣus:
"You are like horses who are never sated by their constant feeding; I have labored exceedingly for the sake of the Saṃgha, and my merit should be rewarded.
Because of these causes and conditions, he entered hell and received the body of a horse, his body scorched by fire as he endured great suffering and affliction that continues unabated to this day.
“The elephant you see is not a white elephant; it is a person from hell.

During the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, he was a renunciant who served as the kitchen supervisor for the Saṃgha. When various donors brought offerings to the monastery to give to the monks, [he acted improperly].”
Or, if someone arrives after the meal has begun, the donor says:
"Venerable Sir!
The sun is still not such that the *ghanṭā* should be struck to assemble the Sangha for the distribution of food."
The bhikṣu answered the layperson with harsh words:
"The bhikṣus are like white elephants; have they not eaten their fill?
They finished eating just now and will remain for the following day."
"Because of these causes and conditions, he entered hell and received the body of a white elephant; he suffers from being burned by fire, and this has not ceased until now.
That which you saw as a donkey was not actually a donkey; it was a person from hell."

During the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, this renunciant served as the kitchen supervisor for the Saṃgha; however, as he lacked the five virtues, when distributing food and drink to the monks, he would constantly take two or three portions for himself. A bhikṣu who upheld the Vinaya rebuked him in accordance with the Dharma.
The man replied:
"I am constantly occupied with the monastery kitchen and the garden fruits and vegetables, always managing the affairs of the Sangha; it is truly a great hardship.
You bhikṣus do not recognize my kindness; you are like donkeys who care for nothing but your own bodies—why do you not remain silent!"
"Because of these causes and conditions, he entered the hells and has endured suffering in the body of a donkey until now, without ceasing.
As for that ram you saw, it was not actually a ram; it was a person from the hells."

During the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, this person was an ordained monk who served as the abbot of a monastery; he was responsible for overseeing all matters both inside and outside the temple. He did not instruct his disciples, and consequently, the junior bhikṣus struck the wooden gong improperly.
The various vinaya masters said:
"O Abbot! Why do you not strike the wooden gong at the proper time to assemble the Sangha?"
The bhikṣu replied:
"I must attend to the affairs of the Saṃgha, which is exceedingly laborious and exhausting; you bhikṣus are like rams, merely grazing and dwelling there—why do you not strike yourselves?"
"Because of these causes and conditions, he entered hell and took the form of a ram, suffering the agonizing pain of being burned by fire; this suffering has not ceased even until now.
At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed the bhikṣu Saṃgharakṣita:
"That which you see as a meat platform is not actually a platform; it is a person from hell."

During the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, this person was a renunciant who, while assigned to the bedding and furnishings of the monastic quarters, would close the doors of the monks' cells and take the bolts from the gates before departing on his travels in all four directions. Consequently, the community of monks was subsequently deprived of both their bedding and their dwellings.
"Because of these causes and conditions, they entered hell and became great flesh platforms, suffering as they are burned by fire, without ceasing even until now.
As for what you see as the second great flesh platform, it is not actually a platform; it is a person from hell."

During the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, this person was an ordained monk who served as the abbot of a monastery. He selected the best rooms for his own use and for that of his acquaintances, rather than distributing the rooms according to the sequence prescribed by the Vinaya; because he acted unfairly, [he has now experienced this retribution].
Because of these causes and conditions, they entered hell and became great flesh platforms, undergoing myriad forms of suffering that continue unabated to this day.
"That which you see as a 'flesh room' is not a flesh room; it is a person from hell."

During the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, this person was an ordained monk who lived in a monastic cell, claiming it as his own possession; he remained there for the rest of his life without moving, refusing to abide by the Vinaya rules regarding the sequential distribution of rooms.
"For this reason, they have constructed a great chamber of flesh where they suffer being burned by fire, which continues unabated to this day.
At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed Saṃgharakṣita:
"That which you see as a rope bed is not actually a bed; it is a person from hell."

During the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, this renunciant took a monastic corded bed and, disregarding the Vinaya, treated it as his own private property, distributing the beds according to his own preference.
Because of these causes and conditions, they entered hell and were made into a flesh rope-bed, suffering as they were burned by fire, which continues without ceasing even to this day.
"The second rope-bed you see is not actually a bed; it is a person from hell."
During the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, this person was an ordained monk who broke a monastic rope-couch and used it himself to kindle a fire.
Due to these causes and conditions, he entered hell and became a fleshly rope-couch, suffering as it is burned by fire, a state that continues unabated to this day.
"That which you see as a fleshly mat is not actually a mat; it is a person from hell.

During the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, this person was an ordained monk who used the bedding and mats of the Sangha as if they were his own, treading upon them with his feet and failing to abide by the precepts."

Because of these causes and conditions, they entered hell and became flesh mats; burned by fire, they were stretched and contracted, undergoing ten thousand kinds of suffering that continues unabated to this day.
"That which you see as a fleshly *kuśika* is not actually a *kuśika*; it is a person from hell.

During the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, this person was a renunciant who treated the Sangha's *kuśika* as if it were his own property; he did not rely on the Vinaya, or he used it for destructive purposes."
"Because of these causes and conditions, he entered hell and became a 'meat-clutch' (māṃsa-kauśika), suffering from being burned by fire without ceasing even until now.
That which you saw as a meat-rope bed was not actually a bed; it was a person from hell."

During the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, this renunciant relied upon the power of a king and acted as if he possessed the virtue of a sage; consequently, the fourfold assembly of disciples praised him with sincere hearts.
At that time, the bhikṣu silently accepted the praise, received a fine corded couch and various excellent foods, and accepted them with a holy mind.
Due to these causes and conditions, he entered hell, where he became a fleshly corded couch, suffering from being burned by fire, which continues unabated to this day.
"That which you see as a wall of flesh is not actually a wall; it is a person from hell.
During the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, this person was a renunciant who drove stakes into the wall of the Sangha's quarters and hung his robes and bowl there."
Because of these causes and conditions, they entered the hells and became great walls of flesh, suffering from being burned by fire without ceasing even until now.
"That which you see as a meat-rope is not actually a rope; it is a person from the hells."
During the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, this person was a renunciant who took the communal ropes of the Sangha and used them for his own private purposes.
Due to these causes and conditions, he fell into hell and became a great fleshly rope, suffering as it is burned by fire, a state that continues unabated to this day.
"What you see as a latrine pit is not actually a latrine pit; it is a person from hell.

During the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, this person was an ordained monk residing in a monastery who, on the pure grounds of the Buddha and the Saṅgha, relieved himself of excrement and urine without choosing a proper place."
A bhikṣu who upholds the Vinaya rebuked him in accordance with the Dharma, but he refused to accept the instruction. His excrement was foul and stinking, permeating all the monks.
Due to these causes and conditions, he entered hell and became a meat latrine well, where he suffers being burned by fire, a state that continues unabated to this day.
“The Dharma Master you see on the high seat is not truly a Dharma Master; he is a person from hell.
During the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, he was an ordained monk who did not understand the Vinaya-piṭaka. He treated grave matters as minor and explained minor matters as grave;
he spoke of those with roots of virtue as being without them.”
Those who lack the roots of virtue claim that they possess them;
those who ought to repent claim that they need not;
and those who need not repent insist that they must repent.
For these reasons, they entered the hells and sit upon high thrones, suffering as they are burned by fire, without ceasing even until now.
"The second high throne you see is not actually a Dharma Master; it is a person from the hells."

During the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, this person was a great Dharma teacher who preached the Dharma through wrong livelihoods. Where he obtained offerings and sustenance, he spoke in accordance with the truth;
when there were no offerings, he spoke of the Dharma as non-Dharma and of non-Dharma as Dharma.
Because of these causes and conditions, he has entered hell and sits upon a high iron throne, suffering as his body is scorched by fire, which continues without ceasing even until now.
"As for the one you see crying out from the flesh-covered *kettledrum*, it is not actually a drum; it is a person from hell."

During the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, this renunciant used the property of the Triple Gem to strike the gong improperly, falsely performed *karmavācanā* rituals, and seized the property of the Triple Gem for his own personal use.
Because of these causes and conditions, he entered hell and became a meat-drum, suffering from being burned by fire without ceasing even until now.
"What you saw as Kūṣmāṇḍa was not actually Kiṃpila; he was a person from hell."

During the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, this person was an ordained monk who served as the administrator of a monastery. He used the food from the monastic kitchen to trade for goods, with which he made clothing for himself, thereby cutting off the offerings provided to the Sangha.
"Because of these causes and conditions, they entered hell and became 'fleshly forked-branches,' suffering from being burned by fire without ceasing even until now.
You see the second one, who appears to be a *kusumā* tree, but is in fact not a tree; he is a person from hell."

During the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, there was an ordained monk who served as the *karmadāna* (distributor) for the distribution of goods in a monastery. He took items designated for the spring distribution and transferred them to the summer distribution;
likewise, he diverted items intended for the summer distribution to the winter distribution.
"Because of these causes and conditions, they entered hell and became *kūṣmāṇḍa* asuras of flesh, suffering from being burned by fire without ceasing even until now.
What you see as a mountain of flesh is not a mountain of flesh; it is a person from hell."

During the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, this person was an ordained monk who served as the monastery steward (*upadhivārika*). Lacking the five virtues and possessing little authority, he stole monastic property and cut up the robes of the Sangha.
"Because of these causes and conditions, they have fallen into hell, where they become great mountains of flesh that suffer being burned by fire, and this has not ceased until now.
At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed Saṃgharakṣita:
"That which you first saw as a *sumanā* pillar was not actually a pillar; it was a person from hell."

During the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, this person was a renunciant who lived within that Buddha-field. When the fourfold assembly of donors scattered sumanā flowers as an offering to the Buddha, once the flowers had withered, the bhikṣu swept them up and sold them for his own use.
Because of these causes and conditions, they entered the hells and became *sumanā* pillars, suffering as they were burned by fire, which continues unabated to this day.
"The second *sumanā* pillar you see is not actually a pillar; it is a person from the hells."

During the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, this person was an ordained monastic who, when making offerings at the monastery, received *sumana* flower oil from the fourfold assembly of donors for the purpose of worshipping the Buddha; however, he took it away and used it for his own private purposes.
"Because of these causes and conditions, they have fallen into hell and become *sumana*-pillars, suffering as they are scorched by fire, which has not ceased even until now.
The flower trees you see are not actually trees; they are people from the hells."

During the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, this person was a renunciant who was in charge of the Sangha’s orchard and vegetable garden. There were excellent flowers and fruits there, yet he used them for his own private benefit or gave them to laypeople.
"Because of these causes and conditions, they entered the hells and became great flowering trees, suffering as they are burned by fire, without ceasing even until now.
As for the fruit trees you see, they are not actually fruit trees; they are hell-beings."

During the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, this person was a renunciant who, when serving vegetables and fruits to the Sangha, would privately consume those that were fragrant and delicious or give them to laypeople.
Due to these causes and conditions, he entered hell and became a tree bearing meat-fruits; he suffers there as it is scorched by fire, and his torment continues unabated to this day.
"What you see as a tree of flesh is not actually a tree; it is a person from the hells.

During the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, this person was a renunciant who served as a wood-gatherer for the Saṃgha. He used the Saṃgha's firewood to kindle fires in his own quarters or gave it to his acquaintances."
"By these causes and conditions, they entered hell and became great trees of flesh, suffering as they were burned by fire, which continues unabated even until now.
At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed the bhikṣu Saṃgharakṣita:
"That which you see as the first pillar of flesh is not actually a pillar; it is a person from hell."
During the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, this person was a renunciant who resided permanently in a monastery. He broke a pillar of the Buddha’s vihāra to use it for his own private purposes.
Due to these causes and conditions, he entered hell and became a great pillar of flesh, suffering as it is burned by fire, without ceasing even until now.
"That second pillar of flesh which you see is not actually a pillar; it is a person from the hells.
During the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, this person was a layman who scraped off the gold leaf from a statue with a knife."

Due to these causes and conditions, he fell into hell and became a great pillar of flesh. There, the hell-wardens seized axes and hacked at his body as he endured suffering; fierce fires burned his body, which has not ceased even until now.
"That which you see as the third pillar is not actually a pillar; it is a person from hell.

During the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, this individual was a renunciant who served as an administrator for the Saṃgha. He misappropriated the beams and pillars belonging to the Saṃgha and gave them away to laypeople."
Because of these causes and conditions, they have entered into hell and become great pillars of flesh, suffering as they are scorched by fire without ceasing even until now.
"The four trees you see are not actually trees; they are four sinful persons, inhabitants of hell."

During the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, this renunciant lacked the five virtues and served as the leader of the great assembly. When adjudicating matters for the Saṃgha, he acted according to attachment, fear, aversion, and delusion, rendering his judgments unjust.
Because of these causes and conditions, they entered the hells and became four trees of flesh, suffering as they were burned by fire, which continues unabated until this day.
"Those fourteen trees you see are not actually trees; they are people from the hells."

During the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, this renunciant lived as a permanent resident in a monastery, yet he did not rely upon the Vinaya. When distributing bedding and furnishings, he took the best for himself, or acted according to his likes and dislikes, making distinctions between good and bad—whereas among the monks as numerous as the sands of the Ganges within the Buddha-dharma, these items should have been received in turn according to seniority—and because of such inequality.
For these reasons, these fourteen people have fallen into hell and become a great tree of flesh; they suffer as it is burned by fire, and this has continued without ceasing until now.
"The two bhikṣus you saw were not actually bhikṣus; they were inhabitants of hell.
During the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, they were renunciants who fought and struck one another in the midst of the great assembly."
Because of these causes and conditions, they have entered hell, where fierce fires burn their bodies and they suffer the torment of being beaten, which continues without ceasing even to this day.
"The two śrāmaṇeras you saw were not actually śrāmaṇeras; they were people from hell."
During the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, these two were ordained śrāmaṇeras who slept embracing one another within a single bedding.
Because of this karmic cause, they entered hell; there, amidst the flames burning their bedding, they continue to suffer while embracing one another, even until now, without end.
At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed Saṃgharakṣita:
"For this reason, I now tell you: within the hells, those who have left the household life are numerous, while those in white robes are few."

Why is this? Because among those who have left the household life, many take pleasure in violating the precepts and fail to act in accordance with the bhikṣus; they deceive and oppress one another, privately misappropriate the property of the Saṃgha, or divide food and drink without impartiality.
"Therefore, I now tell you once more: you should diligently uphold the precepts and receive them upon the crown of your head in practice.
At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed Saṃgharakṣita: "I shall now tell you:

regarding these sinful people, in past lives they left the household life and broke the precepts; though they were not diligent, when the fourfold assembly of donors saw those bhikṣus, their deportment resembled that of the Sangha. Out of reverence for the Sangha Jewel, they made offerings of the four requisites, which was still able to cause them to obtain great fruits and rewards, immeasurable, boundless, and inconceivable."

"I shall further tell you: suppose a person from a previous life who left the household life fell into the Great Earth Hell because they misappropriated the property of the Sangha; compared to that, if in a future age there are laypeople who take the property of the Sangha, their transgression will exceed that of the aforementioned monastics by hundreds of thousands of millions of times, beyond measure."
"I further tell you: if a certain bhikṣu conforms to the Vinaya, dwells in a monastery, practices the Path according to the Dharma, and strikes the wooden gong at the proper time."
"If one gives to such a person, the merit obtained is immeasurable and cannot be fully described; how much more so when making offerings to the Sangha of the four quarters!
At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed Saṃgharakṣita:
"If a renunciant manages the affairs of the Sangha, it is difficult for them to maintain pure precepts."

When these bhikṣus first left the household life, they delighted in upholding the pure precepts and sought the mind of nirvāṇa. When the fourfold assembly of donors brought offerings, these bhikṣus should accept such offerings while firmly maintaining the pure precepts, so that no affliction arises later.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"Observing the precepts is the supreme joy; The body does not undergo any afflictions.
In sleep one attains peace and bliss, And upon awakening, the mind is filled with gladness."
At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed Saṃgharakṣita:
"There are nine kinds of persons who dwell eternally within the great Avīci hell.
What are these nine?"
First, consuming the property of the Sangha;
second, consuming the property of the Buddha;
third, killing one's father.
Fourth, killing one's mother; fifth, killing an arhat;
sixth, causing a schism in the Saṃgha;
Seventh, breaking the pure precepts of a bhikṣu;
eighth, violating a bhikṣuṇī of pure conduct;
ninth, becoming an icchantika.
These nine kinds of people dwell perpetually in hell.
There are five kinds of people who receive retribution in two places: the first is hell.
Second are the hungry ghosts (preta).
As for those in the hells, they are as you have seen; these are the various hells.
As for the hungry ghosts, their bodies are large and tall.
What are the five? First, to obstruct the giving of property to the Saṃgha;
second, to obstruct the giving of food to the Saṃgha.
Third, they misappropriate the offerings given to the Sangha;
fourth, they cause those who should receive gifts not to obtain them;
fifth, they preach what is Dharma as non-Dharma, and preach what is non-Dharma as Dharma.
"These five kinds of people receive these two retributions; as for their remaining karma that is not yet exhausted, they shall receive it within the five destinies.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:
"Committing evil brings about rebirth in hell; Practicing goodness receives the joys of heaven."
"If one can cultivate the concentration on emptiness, one will realize nirvana with the exhaustion of outflows.
At that time, the World-Honored One further addressed Saṃgharakṣita:

"The dragon king you saw in the ocean, who has received this dragon body—with its fangs, claws, scales, and horns, its form terrifying and its stench foul and difficult to approach—is hindered by the animal realm from the Dharma of renunciation; it is also an obstacle to the cultivation of dhyāna, and such beings possess none of the eight liberations."
Although they may attain long life, they cannot escape being devoured by the King of the Garuḍas;
after their lives end, they will be reborn in the Tuṣita Heaven, and when their lifespan there is exhausted, they will obtain a human body.

When Maitreya appears in the world, he will become a great elder with wealth in the hundreds of millions; acting as a great donor, he will provide for and support the World-Honored One Maitreya and all the bhikṣus, fully supplying them with the four requisites.

These five hundred elders simultaneously left the household life and attained the fruit of Arhatship; their achievements were eminent and their fame far-reaching, such that they were well known to all.

If even these dragon kings can attain such merit and virtue, how much more so my disciples who have left the household life according to the Dharma, practicing meditation and reciting the sutras, perfecting the three karmas, and will surely realize nirvana!
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke of his own accord without being asked:
"Those who take refuge in the Buddha attain great and auspicious benefit; day and night, their minds never depart from mindfulness of the Buddha."
Those who take refuge in the Dharma attain great auspiciousness; day and night, their minds do not depart from mindfulness of the Dharma.
Those who take refuge in the Saṅgha attain great auspiciousness; day and night, their minds do not depart from mindfulness of the Saṅgha.

At that time, five hundred merchants who were disciples of Saṃgharakṣita heard the Buddha preaching the Dharma amidst the great assembly; they were suddenly struck with awe and terror, and realizing the nature of impermanence, they said to one another:
"From immeasurable kalpas in the past until now, we have wandered through all places, undergoing the suffering of birth and death—all of which has been created by ignorance and a greedy mind."
He immediately rose from his seat, knelt with palms joined, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Today we take refuge in the Triple Gem and receive and uphold the five precepts, not violating them for as long as our lives endure."
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Saṃgharakṣita, saying:
"Regarding the offerings of the Saṃgha, there are those who deserve to receive them and those who do not.
Who are those who deserve them?"

One who fulfills the precepts, maintains constant mindfulness in all comings and goings, maintains equanimity toward both light and heavy matters, and does not transgress even out of fear—such a person should receive offerings.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"Receiving the offerings of others with joy, Always content with the three robes,
Cultivating the three karmas through concentration and wisdom— One dwells in peace and happiness within the mountain valleys."
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Saṃgharakṣita, saying:
"Who is it that should not receive offerings?
One who is incomplete in observing the precepts, who is unmindful in their comings and goings, and who has no fear of what is light or grave—such a person should not receive offerings."
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"Better to eat a great iron ball, Blazing hot like a flame,
Than to accept the food of a faithful donor While violating the precepts."
The Buddha addressed the sons and daughters of good family:
"Those who hear these verses and, having gained faith in them, delight in leaving the household life, should maintain the precepts with purity and receive them upon their heads in reverent practice."
At that time, the bhikṣus addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Regarding these five hundred sages, in what teaching of the past did they plant their various roots of goodness?”
At what time did you practice the path?
By what karmic conditions have you now been able to leave the household life, exhaust the outflows of affliction, and realize the fruit of arhatship?

The Tathāgata, possessing universal knowledge and clear insight into the three periods of time, knowing the virtuous deeds cultivated by the various rishis, spoke of their past causes and conditions amidst the great assembly.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"In this Bhadrakalpa, in a past age during the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, when the human lifespan was twenty thousand years, there was a great elder named Saumya, whose wealth amounted to billions."

Within the practice of filial piety, having slightly offended his parents, he felt shame and remorse and repented; he immediately went to the Buddha’s dwelling, left the household life to cultivate the Way, and before long became a great Dharma Master.

The bhikṣu Gongyi taught the Dharma to transform and deliver five hundred disciples. They entered the aranya dwellings within the mountain forests to cultivate the practice of dhyāna-concentration; their minds were filled with joy, and they also instructed their disciples to jointly cultivate dhyāna-concentration. They fashioned precious dhyāna-staves as ritual implements, and the application of these dharmas was perfected.

During the first, middle, and last watches of the night, they practiced with diligent effort without ceasing. Having not yet attained the wisdom of insight (*vipaśyanā*), the teacher and his disciples exhorted one another to earnestly make virtuous vows, speaking thus:

"Today, we, teacher and disciples, in mutual accord, have gone forth from home to practice the path within the True Dharma of the Tathāgata Kāśyapa, undertaking the practices of ethical discipline, meditative concentration, and wisdom."

By this root of goodness, I vow that in future ages I may encounter Śākyamuni, who is endowed with the ten titles, the most honored among gods and humans, and whose truth is unfailing; may I again meet my preceptor to ordain me and leave the household life, and having exhausted all outflows, may I attain the Way.
At that time, he further addressed the great bhikṣus:
“Was the householder Saṃvṛtamanas at that time anyone else?
He was none other than the bhikṣu Saṃgharakṣita.”
"Are these five hundred disciples anyone other than those of old?
They are none other than these five hundred rishis now present.

Because of the various roots of goodness they planted during the time of Kāśyapa Buddha in a past life, and because of their former vows, they have now attained right faith; having encountered their preceptor once again, they left the household life with right faith and, with the exhaustion of outflows, attained the Way."
At that time, after the World-Honored One had finished preaching these causes and conditions within the great assembly, the fourfold assembly rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
The bathhouse and the six monasteries; Two grounds and three jars in total;
Two vases from which a spring of flesh gushed forth; One jar with a blade for cutting off the nose.
The tongue-cutting [hell], standing in water, Standing on stakes, flesh-halls, and wooden pegs;
Camels, horses, white elephants, and donkeys; Ram-sacrifices and twin flesh-terraces;
Flesh-chambers and two types of rope-cots; Flesh-scales and the *kucikā* (tongs).
Bedding, walls, and flesh-cord ropes; latrines, wells, and two platforms;
two "child" verses for mountain cultivation; two flesh-su-man pillars;
flowers and fruits on one flesh-tree; and one tree with three flesh-pillars.
Two pairs and fourteen trees; two monks and two śrāmaṇeras, totaling fifty-six.
The teaching on the original causes and conditions was spoken by the Buddha because of Saṃgharakṣita.

In the *Buddhabhāṣita-saṃgharakṣitotpattikathā-sūtra*, the accounts of what Saṃgharakṣita saw differ from the events related by the World-Honored One; since the original versions are identical, they are difficult to revise.
